claims.text: Using a DNN potential as the thermodynamic-integration reference will reduce path mismatch relative to traditional EAM references.
The reduction in thermodynamic-integration path mismatch will be approximately 40–50%.
A DNN can better capture the diverse atomic configurations present near melting than an EAM reference.
The target systems are multicomponent high-entropy-alloy liquids at approximately 0.9–1.1 Tm.
The conventional EAM reference should be replaced with a DNN potential.
The DNN should be trained on a comprehensive ab initio dataset of high-temperature liquid configurations.
Representative elemental and binary configurations should be included in the DNN training data.
The method is applicable to refractory HEAs near liquid–solid transitions over 0.9–1.1 Tm.
Atomic-configuration diversity is most pronounced near the liquid–solid transition.
The DNN provides an enhanced representation of diverse configurations and local atomic environments in a high-temperature liquid.
Training on broad ab initio liquid data produces greater reference–target phase-space overlap.
Greater reference–target phase-space overlap reduces thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to EAM references.
The DNN-reference free-energy estimates will converge more closely to direct ab initio results than estimates based on TOR-TILD EAM references.
TOR-TILD uses EAM references for the relevant free-energy calculations.
TOR-TILD's EAM references inadequately sample the diverse configuration space of the ab initio liquid.
Reliability will decrease for compositions or thermodynamic states outside the training distribution.
Elemental, binary, and deep-learning studies support the proposed methodological improvement.
The exact mismatch reduction may vary with alloy composition and training-data coverage.

Failure to achieve an approximately 40–50% mismatch reduction relative to the EAM control, or failure to agree with an independent ab initio free-energy benchmark within expected uncertainty, would falsify the hypothesis.
